newsitem.title: USA: DC on its way to closing $85 mln deficit - official.
newsitem.headline: DC on its way to closing $85 mln deficit - official.

text.p: District of Columbia is on track to close an $85.4 million shortfall this fiscal year, but declining revenues continue to plague the financially struggling city, D.C.'s chief financial officer said.
"The city is on its way to closing an $85.4 million operating deficit," Anthony Williams told the city's five-member financial control board headed by economist Andrew Brimmer.

"(But)...revenue growth in the District remains virtually flat, and with inflation factored in, revenues are declining," Williams told the board at a hearing on the city's financial progress in the first-quarter of 1997 and on estimated FY 1998 revenue collection in the city.
Williams said the long-term forecast for general sales and use taxes for the city is increasing, but is "still negative in real terms."
He added, however, that the outlook for individual income taxes is "somewhat brighter" because federal government downsizing is finally slowing.

He forecast that average economic growth over the next 10 years will be about two percent lower than the national average. On a bright note, he said federal employment in D.C. will stabilize after 2001 at approximately 200,000 employees.
He added, "Our population will decline to 522,000 persons by the year 2001, then rise slowly, based on Census Bureau projections."
The Bureau announced recently that the city's population continues to plunge. The District lost 11,000 people in the last 12 months, from 554,000 to 543,000, the Bureau said.

Williams said the city "welcomes" three separate sets of recommendations for digging the District out of financial crisis that were made recently by the Clinton Administration, The Brookings Institution, and the Greater Washington Research Center.
He said the city is committed to working with the control board in evaluating each set of proposals "thoroughly."
